lead: An alternating series has terms whose signs flip: plus, minus, plus, minus. If the sizes of the terms shrink steadily to zero, the partial sums cannot run away; they step above and below one limit and close in on it. This gives a quick convergence test that needs no comparison series, and it estimates the error from the first omitted term. It appears in series solutions, Fourier series, and numerical approximations where cancelling terms improve accuracy.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.2 for partial sums and Chapter 3.1 for limits.

blocks.text: An alternating series is a series of the form Σ<sub>n=1</sub><sup>∞</sup> (−1)<sup>n+1</sup> b<sub>n</sub> = b<sub>1</sub> − b<sub>2</sub> + b<sub>3</sub> − b<sub>4</sub> + ⋯, where every b<sub>n</sub> > 0. The factor (−1)<sup>n+1</sup> gives + for n = 1, − for n = 2, + for n = 3, and so on. The number b<sub>n</sub> is the size of the nth term without its sign. The partial sum is S<sub>N</sub> = b<sub>1</sub> − b<sub>2</sub> + ⋯ + (−1)<sup>N+1</sup> b<sub>N</sub>, and the series converges when S<sub>N</sub> tends to a finite limit S as N → ∞. The standard example is the alternating harmonic series 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + ⋯, with b<sub>n</sub> = 1/n. Its sum is ln 2 ≈ 0.693. The first partial sums are S<sub>1</sub> = 1, S<sub>2</sub> = 0.5000, S<sub>3</sub> = 0.8333, S<sub>4</sub> = 0.5833, S<sub>5</sub> = 0.7833, S<sub>6</sub> = 0.6167, S<sub>7</sub> = 0.7595, S<sub>8</sub> = 0.6345, S<sub>9</sub> = 0.7456, S<sub>10</sub> = 0.6456. They jump above and below ln 2 and move closer to it. The plain harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ⋯ diverges, so the minus signs are doing real work.

sections.h3: The Leibnitz test and the remainder bound

blocks.text: Leibnitz test. Suppose bn > 0 for all n, bn+1 ≤ bn for all n (or for all n beyond some N), and bn → 0. Then Σ (−1)n+1 bn converges. The test is also spelled Leibniz; both names mean the same result. Why it works: the even partial sums S2, S4, S6, … increase because S2m − S2m−2 = b2m−1 − b2m ≥ 0. They are bounded above by b1. The odd partial sums S1, S3, S5, … decrease and are bounded below by 0. Each list has a limit. Their gap is S2m − S2m−1 = −b2m → 0, so both lists share one limit S. Remainder estimate: if SN is the Nth partial sum, then |S − SN| ≤ bN+1. The error after stopping is no larger than the first omitted size. The sign of S − SN is the sign of the first omitted term. This test does not say Σ bn converges; that separate idea is absolute convergence, covered in Chapter 3.5.

sections.h3: Using the test and reading its limits

blocks.text: Check the three conditions in order: (1) write b<sub>n</sub> and confirm b<sub>n</sub> > 0; (2) show b<sub>n</sub> → 0; (3) show b<sub>n</sub> decreases, often by comparing b<sub>n+1</sub> with b<sub>n</sub> or by checking the derivative of f(x) with f(n) = b<sub>n</sub>. A failure of any condition means the test gives no conclusion, not that the series diverges. If b<sub>n</sub> does not tend to 0, the terms do not tend to 0, so the series diverges by the nth-term test. If b<sub>n</sub> → 0 but does not decrease, the series may converge or diverge; another test is needed. For example, b<sub>n</sub> = 1/n for odd n and b<sub>n</sub> = 1/n² for even n gives b<sub>n</sub> → 0 but no decrease; the positive odd terms form a divergent harmonic tail, so Σ (−1)<sup>n+1</sup> b<sub>n</sub> diverges. A decrease from some index onward is enough. A finite number of early terms does not affect convergence. Use the remainder bound to stop a computation when b<sub>N+1</sub> is below the required tolerance.

figure.caption: Partial sums of 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − ⋯ step above and below ln 2 and close in on it.

spec.aria: Partial sums of the alternating harmonic series jump above and below the line ln 2 ≈ 0.693 and move closer to it.

examples.question: Test the series Σ<sub>n=1</sub><sup>∞</sup> (−1)<sup>n+1</sup> n/(n²+1) for convergence. Also give b<sub>1</sub>, b<sub>10</sub>, b<sub>100</sub> and f′(2) for f(x) = x/(x²+1), rounded to four decimal places.
steps: The signs alternate because of (−1)<sup>n+1</sup>. Set b<sub>n</sub> = n/(n²+1). For n ≥ 1, b<sub>n</sub> > 0.
Decrease: f′(x) = [(x²+1) − x(2x)]/(x²+1)² = (1−x²)/(x²+1)². For x ≥ 1, 1−x² ≤ 0, so f′(x) ≤ 0. Therefore b<sub>n+1</sub> ≤ b<sub>n</sub>.
The two conditions of the Leibnitz test hold: b<sub>n</sub> decreases and b<sub>n</sub> → 0. The series converges.
examples.answer: The series converges by the Leibnitz test, with b<sub>1</sub> = 0.5000, b<sub>10</sub> = 0.0990, b<sub>100</sub> = 0.0100 and f′(2) = −0.1200.

traps: Checking only b<sub>n</sub> → 0. The Leibnitz test also needs b<sub>n</sub> decreasing; both conditions form the hypothesis.
Using b<sub>N</sub> in the remainder bound instead of b<sub>N+1</sub>. The first omitted term is b<sub>N+1</sub>.
Treating a failed test as a proof of divergence. The Leibnitz test is sufficient only; if decrease fails, another test may still show convergence.
Forgetting b<sub>n</sub> > 0. If b<sub>n</sub> carries its own sign, separate the alternating sign before applying the test.
Mixing the sign start. (−1)<sup>n+1</sup> starts with +, while (−1)<sup>n</sup> starts with −; a shifted sign changes the remainder sign but not convergence.

quiz.q: State the Leibnitz test for an alternating series.
quiz.a: If b<sub>n</sub> > 0, b<sub>n</sub> decreases, and b<sub>n</sub> → 0, then Σ (−1)<sup>n+1</sup> b<sub>n</sub> converges.

quiz.q: The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ⋯ diverges. Why does 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + ⋯ converge?
quiz.a: Here b<sub>n</sub> = 1/n is positive, decreases, and tends to 0. The minus signs make the partial sums step above and below ln 2 by smaller and smaller amounts, so the partial sums converge to ln 2.
Take b<sub>n</sub> = 1/(n+2). It is positive, b<sub>n+1</sub> = 1/(n+3) ≤ 1/(n+2) = b<sub>n</sub>, and b<sub>n</sub> → 0. By the Leibnitz test the series converges.
Take b<sub>n</sub> = (n+1)/n = 1 + 1/n. Then b<sub>n</sub> → 1, not 0. The terms do not tend to 0, so the series diverges by the nth-term test.

quiz.q: For a series that satisfies the Leibnitz test, what is the largest possible error if S<sub>5</sub> is used to estimate S?
quiz.a: The remainder bound gives |S − S<sub>5</sub>| ≤ b<sub>6</sub>. So the error is at most the size of the first omitted term, b<sub>6</sub>.

quiz.q: If b<sub>n</sub> → 0 but b<sub>n</sub> is not decreasing, must Σ (−1)<sup>n+1</sup> b<sub>n</sub> diverge?
quiz.a: No. The Leibnitz test is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. If decrease fails, the test gives no conclusion; the series may converge or diverge, and another test is needed.

quiz.q: Write the remainder estimate for a series that satisfies the Leibnitz test.
quiz.a: |S − S<sub>N</sub>| ≤ b<sub>N+1</sub>, where S is the sum and S<sub>N</sub> is the Nth partial sum.

beyond: Not for the exam. Alternating-series error bounds control truncation in numerical libraries; engineers stop a series when the next term is below tolerance. Fourier series and signal processing use alternating coefficients. Search for 'Leibniz test remainder', 'alternating series error bound', and 'Dirichlet test' next.
